editorial.headline: The Conventional Fintech Behind a Direct Rupiah Loan Match
editorial.standfirst: A conventional fintech peer-to-peer lending service, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali's PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity is a conventional, technology-based lending-and-borrowing intermediary. It provides, manages and operates a financial-service offering that connects lenders with borrowers so they can enter conventional loan agreements. The activity is expressly built around direct rupiah loan agreements made through electronic systems using the internet. Its subject is the service that enables those agreements: bringing the lending and borrowing sides into a structured meeting point, then keeping the financial service available, managed and operating. The scope calls this conventional fintech peer-to-peer lending, but the definition stays concrete. It is the provision, management and operation of a digital financial service for matching lenders and borrowers according to the terms described in the record. Every part of that formulation matters: the service is financial in character, intermediary in function, conventional in the agreements it supports, and internet-based in the way those agreements are made.

That description identifies the registrant in functional terms: the business operating the intermediary service itself. Its task covers the provision, management and operation of the financial-service layer through which borrowers and lenders meet, agree and make the agreement directly in rupiah. The record makes no distinction among the available business scales. Registration is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar, allowing the same defined activity to be registered from the micro scale through the large scale. The breadth of those listed scales does not dilute the description; throughout, the legal-commercial centre remains a conventional loan agreement made directly between lender and borrower through an internet-connected electronic system. Across all four scales, the record preserves one operational description for the service.

Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA and its maximum foreign ownership is 100%. In plain English, the national record allows the activity to be fully foreign owned. The Bali result is equally clear, though it turns on risk rather than a separate ownership figure. Bali assigns it the OK_or_HIGHER_RISK status. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High—which means the activity is not blocked by Bali's moratorium. The moratorium itself blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA across the island on a permanent basis. It does not block this activity. A foreign-owned business can therefore register this activity in Bali today, within the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling.
